headline: High-risk shared-workspace and output-trust pathways: CrewAI can write broad host files while pdf.js reads PDFs, creating medium prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and uses shared memory by default; pdf.js reads PDF files. If CrewAI writes attacker-controlled content into files that pdf.js later processes, the shared filesystem becomes an injection bridge. This is not provably blocked, but it is not a direct default instruction channel either.
conditions: IF CrewAI writes content into a file that pdf.js later opens as input
IF both agents share the same working directory without isolation
mitigations: Run each agent in separate directories
Mount pdf.js inputs read-only
Disable CrewAI file writes for untrusted content
Add a content provenance tag before pdf.js ingestion
requires-engineering: enforce per-file trust labels in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI handles API keys and broad host files, while pdf.js processes PDF documents. If the shared workspace contains sensitive PDFs or crew data, CrewAI can expose them through its broader file access and outbound model/tool calls. pdf.js itself has no network egress, so the main leakage path is via CrewAI.
conditions: IF sensitive PDFs are placed in the shared working directory
IF CrewAI forwards file contents to model providers or tools
mitigations: Keep sensitive PDFs out of the shared workspace
Restrict CrewAI to a least-privilege subdirectory
Disable unnecessary tool integrations
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after testing
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning before outbound calls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: CrewAI has broad filesystem write and subprocess execution, while pdf.js reads PDF files from disk. Their overlapping access to the same workspace can cause write/read races or file clobbering even without git or database writes. The conflict is real in default host-process setups because CrewAI has no self-isolation by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same host directory
IF CrewAI writes files while pdf.js is reading or generating PDFs
mitigations: Use separate per-agent work directories
Serialize access to shared PDFs
Make pdf.js inputs immutable during processing
Run CrewAI in a container with a private volume
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared artifacts

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI can generate outputs from tools and model providers, and pdf.js can consume files in a browser-based workflow. If pdf.js treats CrewAI-produced artifacts as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream document processing. There is no evidence of built-in verification between them, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF pdf.js consumes CrewAI-generated files or text without verification
IF CrewAI outputs are used as source material for document actions
mitigations: Require human review before acting on CrewAI outputs
Add checksum or signature checks on handoff files
Compare extracted PDF text against source documents
Limit pdf.js to rendering, not decision-making
requires-engineering: insert a validation step between agents

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI is documented as handling developer-passed crew data and API keys, while pdf.js processes PDF documents locally with no network egress. No explicit residency or retention mismatch is shown, so compliance risk is limited to local handling gaps rather than a clear policy breach. The other agent is cited because the pair’s data flow is the issue.
conditions: IF regulated PDFs are processed in CrewAI's shared workspace
IF retention or deletion policies differ between crew data and PDF artifacts
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated PDFs in CrewAI workspaces
Document retention for both agents
Delete temporary PDFs after processing
Separate secrets from document inputs
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls
